attribution.note: The sentence follows Marcus's lead-in to the abstract and is in his own voice (the Doctorow aside, then 'What follows is a time capsule'). Either way, he asserts it in his own post. The drafter's flag that it is quoted from the abstract looks doubtful but does not change the attribution.

semantics.note: This is an observation that botshit, as the post defines it, has grown more abundant over time. The proposition and the 'over time' qualifier are preserved.

contract.note: No measure is named. Using a well-tracked proxy (court rulings that found AI hallucinations) for 2023 to mid-2025 is an ordinary, fair reading. The drafter's own flag notes that detection bias may inflate the trend.

evidence.note: Business Insider's counts from Charlotin's database: 10 rulings in 2023, 37 in 2024, 73 in the first five months of 2025. This is a clear rise within the period.
A dated May 2025 summary: 116 cases in the database, 20 of them in May 2025 alone. This shows the pace speeding up just before the post.

reviews.rationale: In the proxy category, documented cases of people submitting false AI-generated content rose steeply from 2023 to mid-2025. Detection bias is a caveat, but no evidence shows the trend was flat or falling. The support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus cites the NYT article and states the takeaway in his own words, endorsing it.

semantics.note: The revision restored his wording, including the 'starting to' hedge and the scope 'on the world stage'. It is an observation about presence, not about decisive impact.

contract.note: The plain reading (AI misinformation documented in elections in several countries, 2024 to mid-2025) is ordinary and suits the low 'starting to' bar.

evidence.note: Benton's dated excerpt of the NYT (June 26, 2025) reports a flood of AI-made fake media of candidates in elections.
The syndicated NYT text cites IPIE: AI used in over 80% of 2024 elections, 215 documented instances, and a harmful role in 69% of cases. These are multi-country tallies.
Romania: officials said an AI-using Russian influence operation tainted the presidential election, and a court annulled the result. This is a concrete international case.
An election law expert calls the headline exaggerated but says the piece catalogs real AI uses in elections. This bears on the headline, not on the narrower claim.

reviews.rationale: Credible reporting with independent IPIE tallies documents AI-generated deceptive content in elections across many countries in 2024–25, including Romania. That meets the low 'starting to see' bar. Disputes over decisive impact do not bear on presence.

attribution.note: These are Marcus's own words in the closing paragraph of his post.

semantics.note: This is a firm, if hyperbolic, causal claim: ChatGPT use harms education and students learn essentially nothing during it. The normalisation is faithful, though 'all too frequent trips' suggests outsourcing episodes.

contract.note: The plain reading (negligible, independently measured learning during ordinary ChatGPT-assisted study, plus harm) is ordinary. The result depends on whether 'essentially nothing' means total learning or added learning, which the speaker did not specify.

evidence.note: A randomized PNAS study (fall 2023): access to unguarded GPT-4 cut unassisted exam performance by 17% versus control. This supports a deleterious effect in that setting, though students still learned something.

Two randomized Python experiments: ChatGPT-access groups gained about 5 questions on unaided post-tests, with no significant difference from controls. This contradicts 'essentially nothing', though the gains are not attributable to the chatbot alone.

reviews.rationale: The harm part holds in one randomized setting: unguarded GPT-4 reduced unaided math performance. The general 'learning essentially nothing' part is not borne out: in the coding RCTs, ChatGPT-access students made substantial independent gains comparable to controls. Evidence of harm extends beyond one setting only weakly.

semantics.note: This is an observation that o3 produced a plausible but partly fabricated financial document, as Axios reported. Reading 'financial report' as a briefing with financial metrics is fair.

contract.note: The criteria track his words directly: an Axios report, o3, and a mix of real and fabricated or unverifiable financial content.

evidence.note: The archived Axios AI+ newsletter of July 3, 2025 names o3 and describes the Wealthfront briefing that cited a made-up investor deck.
Axios could not verify the deck or the metrics. The figures differed from prior reporting, and the banks named were not advising the firm.
Axios says the output combined verified metrics with unverified ones, which matches 'blend of truth and bullshit'.

reviews.rationale: The Axios newsletter of July 3, 2025 reports that o3 produced a credible-seeming Wealthfront briefing that mixed verified financial figures with unverifiable metrics and a fabricated investor deck. That matches the claim.
